title: Disability Sport as Institution
bigQuestion: What turns games for disabled athletes from a kind gesture into a real institution with rules, records and rights?

story.title: The Card Beside the Chair
story.kicker: Before the race starts, a small card decides which race a teenager is in.
paragraphs: It is a spring Saturday at a junior track meet in Champaign, Illinois. A row of racing wheelchairs sits beside the track. Each has three wheels and a long, low frame. They look nothing like the chairs people use at home or at school.

A fourteen-year-old racer named Maya checks in at a folding table. The official asks for her classification card. The card lists her name, her sport and her sport class: T54. The T stands for track. The number tells the official which group of wheelchair racers she belongs with.

Maya's older cousin came along to watch. "Why does a race need a card?" he asks. Maya explains that trained classifiers looked at how her body works before she ever raced here. They placed her with athletes whose impairments affect racing in a similar way. That way, the race measures training and speed.

Across the track hangs a banner for the University of Illinois wheelchair track team. Maya's coach tells her cousin that the university has run wheelchair sports since 1948. Some of the fastest racers in the world trained on this campus. Several won the Boston Marathon and Paralympic gold medals.

The starter calls the T54 race. Maya tucks her card into her bag and rolls to the line. Her cousin looks at the card again. It is a small piece of paper. Yet behind it stand a rule book, a world federation and more than seventy years of history.
story.think: Why might a sport need a written system for deciding who races against whom?

sections.title: Deaf Sport Builds Its Own Games

lessons.title: Schools for the Deaf
lessons.mainIdea: Schools for deaf students, like the one in Jacksonville, Illinois, became the first homes of Deaf sport in the United States.
reading: In 1817, Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc opened a school for deaf students in Hartford, Connecticut. Clerc was a deaf teacher from France. Today it is called the American School for the Deaf. It was the first lasting school of its kind in the United States.

Other states soon built their own. The Illinois legislature created a state school for deaf students in Jacksonville in 1839. Many deaf children lived at these *residential schools* during the school year. The schools had playgrounds, gyms and teams, and their students played other schools.

In 1864, President Abraham Lincoln signed a law that allowed a college for deaf students in Washington, D.C. It later took the name Gallaudet. Graduates of the deaf schools formed clubs in big cities. These clubs held dances, meetings and sports leagues. Many members see themselves as part of a *Deaf community*, with its own language and culture.

words.d: a school where students live during the school year; many early schools for deaf students worked this way
people who share sign language and Deaf culture; the capital D names the culture, not only hearing loss

lessons.title: Paris, 1924
lessons.mainIdea: Deaf athletes from nine nations met in Paris in 1924 for the first International Silent Games, the start of the Deaflympics.
reading: Eugène Rubens-Alcais was a deaf Frenchman who led a sports club for deaf athletes. He wanted deaf athletes to meet across borders. With Antoine Dresse of Belgium, he organized the *International Silent Games*. They were held in Paris in August 1924.

The timing mattered. Paris had just hosted the Summer Olympic Games that year. About 148 deaf athletes from nine European nations came to the Silent Games. They competed in events such as track and field, cycling, swimming and soccer.

After the games, leaders founded a governing body. It was known by its French initials, *CISS*, for the International Committee of Sports for the Deaf. It is the oldest international body for disabled athletes. Deaf athletes ran it themselves from the start, which made it unusual.

words.d: the first world games for deaf athletes, held in Paris in 1924
the French initials of the International Committee of Sports for the Deaf, founded in 1924

lessons.title: The Deaflympics Today
lessons.mainIdea: The Deaflympics have their own rules and body, and deaf sport chose to stay separate from the Paralympic movement.
reading: The International Olympic Committee recognized the deaf sports committee in 1955. In 2001, the games took the name *Deaflympics*. The body is now called the International Committee of Sports for the Deaf, or ICSD. Winter Deaflympics have been held since 1949, when they began in Seefeld, Austria.

The Deaflympics have their own entry rule. An athlete must have a hearing loss of at least 55 *decibels* in the better ear. A decibel is a unit that measures how loud a sound is. Athletes may not wear hearing aids or implants while they compete.

Races start with lights and signals that athletes can see. The deaf sports committee joined the Paralympic movement for a time, then left in 1995. Its leaders argued that deaf athletes share a language and culture more than an impairment. They chose to keep their own games.

words.d: the world games for deaf athletes, called by that name since 2001
a unit that measures how loud a sound is
the International Committee of Sports for the Deaf, the world body that runs the Deaflympics

lessons.title: Veterans Come Home
lessons.mainIdea: After World War II, veterans with spinal cord injuries formed the first wheelchair basketball teams in 1946.
reading: Before World War II, most people with a *spinal cord injury* lived only a short time. Infections often killed them. During and after the war, new medicines like penicillin changed that. Thousands of wounded soldiers came home and lived for decades.

Better chairs helped too. In 1933, Harry Jennings and Herbert Everest designed a folding steel wheelchair. It was lighter than the heavy wooden chairs of the past. Chairs like it could fit in a car and move across a gym floor.

In 1946, veterans in hospitals run by the Veterans Administration began playing basketball from wheelchairs. Teams formed in California and Massachusetts. By the late 1940s, a California team called the Flying Wheels toured the country. Crowds paid to watch. The *veterans* wanted real games, not pity.

words.d: damage to the nerves in the backbone that can affect movement and feeling below the injury
people who have served in the armed forces
the U.S. agency, set up in 1930, that ran hospitals and benefits for former soldiers

look.title: Two chairs side by side
look.text: One chair is made of wood with a cane seat. It is heavy and does not fold. The other is made of steel tubes. It folds flat and weighs much less. The second design came from Jennings and Everest in 1933.

lessons.title: Tim Nugent at Galesburg
lessons.mainIdea: In 1949, Tim Nugent of the University of Illinois hosted the first national wheelchair basketball tournament in Galesburg, where the NWBA was founded.
reading: In 1948, the University of Illinois opened a program for students with disabilities. It began at a branch campus in Galesburg, Illinois. Many students were veterans. The program's leader was Timothy Nugent, a young veteran himself.

Nugent believed disabled students should take part in all of college life, including sport. In April 1949, he hosted the first National Wheelchair Basketball Tournament in Galesburg. Teams came from several states. At that meeting, the players and coaches founded the *National Wheelchair Basketball Association*, or NWBA.

The NWBA wrote rules, kept records and ran a yearly tournament. That is what a *governing body* does. When the Galesburg campus closed, Nugent's program moved to the main campus in Urbana-Champaign. Its basketball team became known as the Gizz Kids.

words.d: the U.S. body for wheelchair basketball, founded at Galesburg, Illinois, in 1949
an organization that writes a sport's rules, runs its events and keeps its records

rows: International Sports Organization for the Disabled

look.prompt: Which body on this list was founded in Illinois, and how many years before the IPC?

check.why: A governing body sets a sport's rules and runs its events and records, like the NWBA.

check.q: Who led the University of Illinois program for students with disabilities?
check.why: Timothy Nugent led the program that began at Galesburg in 1948.

lessons.title: A Campus That Made Room
lessons.mainIdea: The University of Illinois changed its buildings for wheelchair users, and its athletes went on to win world races.
reading: Nugent did not only coach. He pushed the Urbana-Champaign campus to add ramps and *curb cuts*. A curb cut is a slope where a sidewalk meets the street. He also led research for the first national standard for buildings wheelchair users could enter, published in 1961.

A campus that people can reach sets the stage for athletes. Nugent's program grew into a unit now called Disability Resources and Educational Services, or DRES. Its wheelchair basketball and track teams still compete for the university. Nugent died in 2015 at age 92.

Its racers became famous. Jean Driscoll studied at Illinois and won the women's wheelchair race at the Boston Marathon eight times. Tatyana McFadden, born in Russia in 1989, also trained there. She won many Paralympic medals in track races. Both are known for helping make *wheelchair racing* a sport people follow.

words.d: a small ramp where a sidewalk meets the street, so wheels can roll across
how easily a place can be reached and used by people with disabilities
road and track races for athletes in specially built racing chairs

look.title: A slope in the sidewalk
look.text: Walk to a street corner near your school. Look at where the sidewalk meets the road. Many corners now have a gentle slope with bumps on it. In the 1940s, almost none did. The University of Illinois was one of the first campuses to add them.
look.prompt: How might a curb cut be part of sports history, even though no game is played there?

check.q: What is a curb cut?
choices: a cut in a racing chair
a small ramp where a sidewalk meets the street
check.why: A curb cut is a slope that lets wheels roll from sidewalk to street.

check.q: How many times did Jean Driscoll win the women's wheelchair race at the Boston Marathon?
check.why: Jean Driscoll, who studied at Illinois, won the Boston wheelchair race eight times.

check.why: Nugent led research for the first national building standard, published in 1961.

sections.title: From Hospital Lawn to World Games

lessons.title: Guttmann's Hospital Games
lessons.mainIdea: Ludwig Guttmann used sport at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, and his games became international in 1952.
reading: Ludwig Guttmann was a Jewish doctor in Germany. In 1939, he fled Nazi rule and moved to England. In 1944, he opened a center for spinal injuries at Stoke Mandeville Hospital. Doctors elsewhere often expected such patients to stay in bed.

Guttmann believed sport was part of *rehabilitation*, the work of regaining strength and skills after an injury. His patients played in the hospital's grounds. In 1948, he held an archery contest there. The Stoke Mandeville Games then met every year.

In 1952, a team of Dutch veterans traveled to take part. That made the games *international*, meaning more than one nation competed. More countries joined through the 1950s. The games soon needed a federation to write rules and plan each year's events.

words.d: the work of regaining strength and skills after an injury or illness
involving more than one nation

look.title: A bed or a bow
look.text: It is 1948 in an English hospital. Some doctors say a man with a spinal injury should rest in bed. Dr. Guttmann says he should be out on the lawn with a bow and arrows, aiming at a target. Both are trying to help the patient.
look.prompt: What did Guttmann believe sport could do that rest could not?

check.why: Rehabilitation is the work of regaining strength and skills after an injury or illness.

lessons.title: Rome, Then Toronto
lessons.mainIdea: The first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960 were for wheelchair athletes; Toronto in 1976 opened the doors to more groups.
reading: In 1960, Guttmann's games were held in Rome, soon after the Olympics there. Only athletes who used wheelchairs could enter. Wheelchair basketball, swimming and archery were on the program. Wheelchair basketball has been part of every Summer Paralympics since.

Other disabled athletes were still left out. At Toronto in 1976, amputees and blind athletes competed for the first time. That same year, Örnsköldsvik, Sweden, hosted the first Winter Paralympic Games. Athletes with cerebral palsy joined the Summer Games in 1980.

The name *Paralympic* uses the Greek word para, meaning beside. It says the games run beside the Olympics. At Seoul in 1988, the Paralympics used the same venues as the Olympics. That became the normal pattern. Each *impairment* group had once needed its own door; now more doors were open.

words.d: describing the world games for athletes with physical and visual impairments; para means beside
a difference in how part of the body or senses work, such as low vision or limb loss
a person who is missing part or all of an arm or leg

lessons.title: One Committee for the World
lessons.mainIdea: The International Paralympic Committee, founded in 1989, brought many separate federations under one governing body.
reading: By the 1980s, several world bodies ran disabled sport. Each served one group. One served wheelchair athletes. The International Sports Organization for the Disabled, founded in 1964, served amputees and others. The International Blind Sports Federation began in 1981. These bodies had to agree on every Games.

In 1982, they formed a *coordinating* committee to plan together. It was not enough. On September 22, 1989, in Düsseldorf, Germany, leaders founded the *International Paralympic Committee*, or IPC. Its offices are in Bonn, Germany. It runs the Paralympic Games and sets rules for many sports.

In 2001, the IPC and the International Olympic Committee signed an agreement. It said a city chosen for the Olympics would also host the Paralympics. The rule took effect for the 2008 Games in Beijing. Each country also has a *national Paralympic committee* that picks its teams.

words.d: the world governing body of the Paralympic movement, founded in 1989
working together so separate groups plan as one
a country's body that enters athletes in the Paralympic Games

look.prompt: What problem did the IPC solve when it was founded in 1989?

lessons.title: A Letter and a Number
lessons.mainIdea: Classification groups Paralympic athletes by how their impairment affects their sport, so each event is a fair contest.
reading: Paralympic athletes compete in *sport classes*. A sport class groups athletes whose impairments affect their sport in a similar way. Without classes, results would show mostly who has the least impairment. With them, results show training and skill.

Class names use a letter and a number. In track, T means track and F means field. In swimming, the letter is S. The number shows the type of impairment and how much it affects the sport. For example, T11 to T13 are for runners with low or no vision. T51 to T54 are wheelchair racing classes.

Trained officials called *classifiers* decide each class. They include doctors, therapists and sport experts. The IPC first adopted an Athlete Classification Code in 2007 and revised it in 2015. Athletes may be checked again as they grow or as rules change.

words.d: a group of Paralympic athletes whose impairments affect their sport in a similar way
a trained official who decides which sport class an athlete belongs in
the system of placing athletes in sport classes

check.q: What is the purpose of sport classes?

lessons.title: Soldier Field, July 1968
lessons.mainIdea: The first Special Olympics Summer Games were held at Soldier Field in Chicago in 1968, with the help of the Chicago Park District.
reading: In 1962, Eunice Kennedy Shriver held a summer day camp at her Maryland home. It was for children with *intellectual disabilities*. In that era, many such children were kept out of schools and sports. Shriver wanted them to have a place to play and compete.

In Chicago, a park district teacher named Anne McGlone Burke had a similar idea. She proposed a citywide track meet. With support from the Kennedy Foundation and the Chicago Park District, it grew. On July 20, 1968, the first International *Special Olympics* Summer Games opened at Soldier Field.

About 1,000 athletes came from across the United States and Canada. Special Olympics is its own movement, apart from the Paralympics. It groups athletes by ability, age and sex in a system called *divisioning*. Burke later served on the Illinois Supreme Court.

words.d: the sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities, whose first Summer Games were held in Chicago in 1968
a disability that affects learning and reasoning, and everyday living skills, that begins in childhood
the Special Olympics system of grouping athletes by ability, age and sex

lessons.title: From Posters to Laws
lessons.mainIdea: Disability sport moved from charity campaigns toward legal rights through laws passed from 1973 to 1998.
reading: Starting in 1946, the March of Dimes chose a national *poster child* each year to raise money against polio. Such campaigns raised money but showed disabled people as objects of pity. Many disabled activists wanted rights, not pity. In 1977, they held a sit-in of more than three weeks in a federal building in San Francisco.

The sit-in pushed the government to enforce *Section 504* of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. Section 504 bans discrimination based on disability in programs that get federal money. Public schools and colleges get federal money, so their sports are covered. The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 also asked the U.S. Olympic Committee to include disabled athletes.

President George H. W. Bush signed the *Americans with Disabilities Act*, or ADA, on July 26, 1990. It covers public places, including gyms, pools and stadiums. In 1998, Congress amended the sports law to give the Olympic committee duties for Paralympic athletes. In 2019, it became the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee.

part of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 that bans disability discrimination in federally funded programs
the 1990 federal law that bans disability discrimination in public life, including public places
